html:
The traditional Mongolian script is the alphabet that Genghis Khan had adopted for the Mongolian language around 1204, borrowed from the Uyghurs. It is written in vertical lines, top to bottom, and is still used today.

Until then the Mongols had no writing. According to the story, when Genghis defeated the Naimans in 1204 his men captured a Uyghur scribe named Tata-tonga, who carried the Naiman ruler's seal. Genghis had him teach his sons to write Mongolian in the Uyghur letters. The old Uyghur script itself came from the Sogdian alphabet, which goes back to Aramaic.

Writing let the new empire keep records, issue orders and write laws. The Secret History of the Mongols was first written in it.

  • In the 1600s the Manchus adapted it to write their own language.
  • In the 1940s the communist government of Mongolia replaced it with the Cyrillic alphabet.
  • In Inner Mongolia, in China, it never stopped being used.

After 1990 Mongolia brought it back into schools and has moved toward using it alongside Cyrillic in official documents.
